Cramped atoms and letter spacing in NAEE

Features of interest · NAEE book links

An atom is a written form between spaces or maqaf marks. These examples show shapes that can feel cramped in Taamey D even when no ink overlaps. An atom can belong to more than one family. The families group candidates for visual judgment rather than providing an exhaustive inventory of cramped atoms.

Each row compares the same complete atom at usual spacing and with 0.06em extra letter spacing. The Reference opens the verse in NAEE. Current NAEE states which spacing the edition currently applies. The broader trial families do not yet change automatic spacing.

  1. A broad vowel and accent on a narrow letter
  2. Adjacent narrow letters, both with marks below
  3. Qof and its predecessor, both with marks below

A broad vowel and accent on a narrow letter

A yod, vav or final nun carries a broad below-letter vowel and a below-letter accent. The vowel dots and accent share a narrow letter’s space. This is the family already expanded automatically in NAEE.

Adjacent narrow letters, both with marks below

Two adjacent narrow letters each carry marks below. Broad vowel dots or an extra mark below a letter leave less room between the sets of marks. These examples include vav beside yod and nun beside vav. This broader family is a trial for possible expansion of the automatic rule.

נִ֣ינְוֵ֔ה נִ֣ינְוֵ֔ה Genesis 10:11 Body text Usual spacing
וַיֵּ֔לֶךְ וַיֵּ֔לֶךְ Genesis 22:3 Body text Usual spacing

Qof and its predecessor, both with marks below

The letter immediately before qof in reading order and qof itself both have marks below. Qof’s descending stroke adds to the crowding around those marks. The examples include broad vowel dots on the predecessor, an extra below-letter accent on qof, and an extra below-letter accent on the predecessor. This family is also a trial for possible expansion of the automatic rule.
